competitors.title: Durable Execution — Diagrid Catalyst Docs
key_points: Event sourcing model: every workflow step is an append-only history log (WorkflowStarted, ActivityScheduled, ActivityCompleted, TimerFired, ExternalEventReceived)
Deterministic replay: on crash, re-runs orchestrator from the top, replaying history events sequentially instead of restoring snapshot
Activities are the escape hatch for non-deterministic operations; must be idempotent for at-least-once guarantees
Continue-as-new bounds unbounded history for long-running workflows (monitor loops, long-running agents)
Durable timers and external events enable zero-cost waiting for human approvals, webhooks, and scheduled pauses
Child workflows for sub-processes that need their own durability (timers, retries, external events)

competitors.title: How Inngest Functions Execute — Durable Execution Docs
key_points: Step-based memoization: each step runs once, result persisted; subsequent executions skip completed steps by injecting stored results
Each step executes as a separate HTTP request; no custom runtime rules or worker management needed
Built-in flow control: concurrency, priority, throttling, rate limiting, idempotency — available in all environments
Supports serve (serverless HTTP endpoints) or connect (persistent workers); no separate infrastructure to manage
Self-hostable as single binary with SQLite or Postgres — vs Temporal's multi-component cluster requirement
step.run, step.sleep, step.waitForEvent, step.invoke primitives for durable workflow composition

competitors.title: Temporal Workflows — Platform Documentation
key_points: Event history as source of truth: complete ordered log of Commands and Events for each workflow execution
Deterministic replay: workflow restarts from beginning, replays event history step-by-step to rebuild state without redoing work
Replay-safe operations: Time from workflow context, durable timers as events, activities handle all I/O (API calls, DB, LLM invocations)
History limit: 51,200 events / 50MB per workflow; Continue-As-New to bound growth
Multi-language SDKs: Go, Java, TypeScript, Python — same code runs in development and production
Workflows can run for years across infrastructure failures; Temporal Server cluster or Temporal Cloud required

Combines Restate and Langfuse for agent reliability, observability, and quality control in one stack

competitors.title: Build Reliable AI Agents with Durable Execution — Pydantic AI + DBOS

competitors.title: Build AI Agents That Resume from Failure with Pydantic AI + Prefect

Saves hundreds of dollars/month at scale by avoiding re-execution of expensive LLM calls after partial failures
Prefect + Pydantic AI integration for stateful, durable AI agent workflows
Task-level retry policies with exponential backoff; flow-level state persistence across crashes

angles: Checkpointing is NOT enough: Restate's argument that agents are distributed applications requiring durable execution (event sourcing + replay), not just periodic snapshots
Two programming models: step-based memoization (Inngest) vs deterministic replay (Temporal, Diagrid) — different tradeoffs for developer experience vs runtime guarantees
The hidden cost of non-durable agents: GPU waste ($17.75/crash), LLM token burn ($800 reasoning loops), and how durable execution pays for itself within weeks
Deterministic replay constraints: the single most important rule of durable execution — everything non-deterministic goes in activities, orchestrators are pure functions
Framework-agnostic durability: Diagrid Catalyst supports 9+ agent frameworks making any framework crash-proof without rewriting agent logic
Postgres-native durable execution: DBOS and Inngest offer simplicity for teams already running Postgres — no infrastructure additions needed
Human-in-the-loop without polling: durable timers and external events enable zero-cost waiting for approvals, webhooks, and user actions over days without compute
Agent failure mode taxonomy: step repetitions (17.14%), reasoning-action mismatches (13.98%), tool misuse (most common) — each addressable by different checkpointing strategies
outline: Introduction: Why Simple Checkpointing Isn't Enough for Production AI Agents
The Problem: What Happens When an Agent Crashes Mid-Flight
GPU cost waste per crash ($17.75 without checkpointing, $1.27 with 15-min intervals)
Hidden token burns ($800 reasoning loops undetected by standard monitoring)
8-13% correctness for chat-only recovery vs 100% with semantics-aware checkpoint/restore
Durable Execution Models Compared
Event sourcing + deterministic replay (Diagrid/Dapr, Temporal, DBOS)
Step-based memoization (Inngest)
Virtual objects + journaling (Restate)
Task caching + flow persistence (Prefect)
The Determinism Requirement: The Non-Negotiable Rule
What you CANNOT do in orchestrator code (random, UUID, current time, I/O, blocking)
What you CAN do (in-memory computation, activities, durable timers, external events)
Activities: The Escape Hatch for the Real World
Idempotency requirement: at-least-once semantics demand idempotent external operations
Activity retry policies: zero retries for payments, exponential backoff for flaky APIs
Programming Model Tradeoffs: Memoization vs Replay
Inngest: step-based memoization with standard language primitives, no custom runtime
Temporal/Diagrid: deterministic replay with strict runtime rules but stronger guarantees
Restate: virtual objects with exactly-once semantics, no idempotency keys needed
DBOS: Postgres-native durable execution with zero infrastructure overhead
Checkpointing Strategies for AI Agent-Specific Failures
Tool-call durability: recording tool invocations in history, replaying from cache
Replay-safe LLM calls: wrapping non-deterministic LLM invocations in activities
Multi-agent coordination: child workflows with independent durable histories
Human-in-the-loop patterns: durable timers and external events for zero-cost waiting
Bounding History for Long-Running Agents
Continue-as-New (Temporal, Diagrid): truncating history at generation boundaries
History limits: 51,200 events / 50MB per Temporal workflow
Inngest's step-based approach naturally limits per-step state
Infrastructure Comparison: Self-Hosting and Scaling
Inngest: single binary + SQLite/Postgres — $15-50/month CPU orchestrator
Temporal: multi-component cluster + Cassandra/Postgres — requires Temporal Cloud or heavy ops
Diagrid: managed Catalyst with Dapr open-source runtime, consumption-based billing
Restate Cloud: SOC 2, HIPAA, enterprise SSO, consumption-based
DBOS: Postgres-native, lowest operational overhead
Agent Framework Integration
Diagrid Catalyst: 9+ frameworks (CrewAI, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents, Google ADK, Pydantic AI, etc.)
LangGraph v1.2: built-in Saga patterns with error_handler parameter
Pydantic AI + DBOS/Prefect: type-safe durable agent frameworks
Cost Analysis: Does Durable Execution Pay for Itself?
GPU waste avoided ($17.75 per crash)
LLM token costs saved ($800 reasoning loops, $0.06 per failed 10-call chain)
Orchestrator overhead ($15-50/month CPU) vs GPU savings ($5-15/hr per card)
Security and Compliance Considerations
Restate: SOC 2, HIPAA, enterprise SSO, client-side encryption (Feb 2026)
Inngest: SOC 2 Type II compliant
Diagrid/Catalyst: enterprise-grade with self-hosted options
Practical Implementation Guide: Choosing Your Approach
Small team, already on Postgres: DBOS or Inngest (self-hosted)
Enterprise with multi-framework agents: Diagrid Catalyst
Long-running orchestrations (months/years): Temporal or Diagrid
Serverless-first team: Inngest (native serverless support)
GPU-intensive agent workloads: any durable execution + checkpointing every 15 minutes
Future Trends: Agent Checkpointing Beyond 2026
Standardization of durable execution APIs across agent frameworks
Checkpoint-aware LLM inference (resumable token generation)
Cross-cloud durable execution as a default expectation for production agents
